haiku-low.q1: Start, then pages of 500 by ascending id, one at a time, never in parallel. Then catch-up on changes, then swap. No parallel fetching.
haiku-low.q2: In sync_state.cursor, the id of the last product on the last fully saved page. Page and cursor are saved in one transaction, so they stay consistent.
haiku-low.q3: start_seq is taken before the first page. Catch-up fetches changes since start_seq and applies them by change_seq, so later edits and deletes replace or remove copied rows.
haiku-low.q4: The server returns HTTP 410. Catch-up clears state and restarts the download; incremental sets mode full and re-downloads on Wi-Fi. products keeps serving reps.
haiku-low.q5: Built in products_staging by pages of 500, then caught up. It replaces products in one transaction once no catalogue read is open.
haiku-low.q6: App launch or return to foreground, when mode is incremental and last_attempt_at is over 15 minutes old or unset. Wi-Fi return does not trigger it.
haiku-low.q7: Retries network errors and 5xx with waits of 2, 4, 8, 16 seconds, five attempts total. Then it stops, keeps saved data, and waits for the next trigger.
haiku-low.q8: The page in flight finishes and saves, then the download pauses. No new page starts until Wi-Fi returns, and it resumes from cursor.
haiku-low.q9: It compares change_seq with the stored row for the same id. It applies the item if no row exists or its change_seq is higher; otherwise it skips.
haiku-low.q10: It starts from sync_state.last_seq and requests changes since that value. last_seq advances in the same transaction as each applied batch of items.
haiku-low.q11: NOT STATED for what the server reads. The feed returns products and tombstones with change_seq above since. Deletes are tombstones with deleted=true, kept 7 days.

sonnet.q1: It is split into pages of up to 500 live products, fetched with keyset pagination (id above the last page's last id, in id order). Pages are fetched one at a time, never in parallel. A page with fewer than 500 products (or an empty page) is the last.
sonnet.q2: The resume position is the cursor (id of the last product on the last fully saved page) in the sync_state row in the app's SQLite database. Each page's products are applied to products_staging and the cursor is saved in the same transaction, so a page and its cursor are saved together or not at all. A page interrupted mid-way rolls back and is fetched again after the saved cursor.
sonnet.q3: POST /catalogue/full/start returns start_seq (the highest change_seq) before the first page. After the last page, catch-up calls /catalogue/changes?since=catch_up_seq (starting at start_seq) in batches of 1000, applying each item to staging with the apply rule (applied only if no stored row or the item's change_seq is higher). Later edits replace the page copy, equal copies are skipped, later deletes arrive as tombstones that remove the row, and re-creations come back as inserts. Only after catch-up finishes does the swap happen.
sonnet.q4: The server returns HTTP 410 (resync required; 410 is this plan's choice). The client does not retry it. During catch-up (step 3), it clears start_seq, cursor and catch_up_seq and goes to step 1, which empties staging; mode stays full. During incremental sync (step 5), it sets mode to full, clears start_seq and cursor, and goes to step 1 (needs Wi-Fi). products keeps serving reps until the swap.
sonnet.q5: It is built in products_staging: step 1 creates and empties it, pages and catch-up are applied to it, and products is not touched meanwhile. It becomes the live catalogue at the swap (step 4), once the last catch-up response had fewer than 1,000 items and no catalogue read is open. In one SQLite transaction, products is dropped, products_staging is renamed to products, last_seq is set to catch_up_seq, mode becomes incremental, and start_seq, cursor and catch_up_seq are cleared.
sonnet.q6: App launch or return to the foreground, with mode incremental, and last_attempt_at either never set or more than 15 minutes ago. Wi-Fi returning does not trigger it. Any network may be used. It runs only in the foreground, and not while mode is full.
sonnet.q7: It retries the same request after 2 s, 4 s, 8 s and 16 s, five attempts in total. After the fifth failure it stops, keeps everything already saved, and waits for the next trigger. For a download the next trigger is launch, foreground or Wi-Fi return. For incremental sync it is launch or foreground at least 15 minutes after last_attempt_at.
sonnet.q8: The page in flight finishes and is saved, then the download pauses. No new page starts until Wi-Fi returns, and then it continues from the saved cursor.
sonnet.q9: It applies the apply rule: compare the item's change_seq with the stored row for the same product id. If there is no stored row, or the item's change_seq is higher, apply it (a product inserts or replaces the row, a tombstone deletes it). Otherwise skip it. A tombstone with no stored row changes nothing.
sonnet.q10: It starts from last_seq, calling GET /catalogue/changes?since=<last_seq>&limit=1000. last_seq is saved in the same transaction as the applied items of each response (set to the last change_seq applied), so it moves forward with every batch. It repeats while responses have 1,000 items. After the swap, last_seq is set to catch_up_seq.
sonnet.q11: NOT STATED for what the server reads internally. The document says only that the change feed returns products and tombstones with change_seq above since, in change_seq order. Deletes are represented as tombstones (rows kept with deleted = true, purged after 7 days). change_seq is stamped from a global Postgres sequence on each insert, update and delete.
